To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
obese children consumed more calories than lean children in response to increased feeding frequency, but that lean children consumed less calories in response to increased frequency.
obese and normal weight children differed in appetite responses to feeding frequency and that obese children were not as responsive to subjective fullness as normal weight children.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of feeding frequency on energy intake in obese and normal weight children.
the role of meal pattern in the development and maintenance of obesity in children.
the effects of feeding pattern on appetite in lean and obese prepubertal subjects.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
feeding frequency and weight group are important factors in determining food intake in prepubertal obese children.
meal pattern affects satiety in children and that the effect may be more marked in NW children.
the feeding frequency has no effect on appetite in obese prepubertal girls.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
obese children are not more satiated than normal weight children, but they do not restrict intake based on their subjective sense of fullness, as normal weight children do.
the effect of meal frequency on satiety and food intake may differ in obese and non‐obese subjects and that the effect of feeding pattern may differ in children and adults.
meal frequency is not an important determinant of appetite in OB children, but it may be important in NW children.
The main takeaway from our work is that
feeding frequency may be important in the management of obesity.
the effect of meal frequency on appetite and food intake is not the same in lean and obese children.
meal frequency and timing may be an important factor in weight gain in children and should be considered when developing strategies to prevent childhood obesity.
